headline: Okkanai is uncertain: perhaps from archaic おおけなし (ookenashi, “impudent, undisciplined”), or from おっかながる (okkanagaru, “to be afraid, be nervous”).
Kanjin is 肝 (kan, “liver”) plus 腎 (jin, “kidney”), with 心 a daiyōji replacing 腎.
Totte is a sound shift from 取りて (torite).
Ikanimo is いかに (ikani) plus も (mo).
Konomashii is the verb 好む (konomu, “to prefer, to like”) made into an adjective with the suffix しい (-shii).
Shiba is from Old Japanese, one of the oldest attested words in the language, used in the Man'yōshū and Nihon Shoki.
Kokochi is a sound shift from 心持ち (kokoromochi, “nature; feeling, mood”), and its kanji spelling is an ateji.
Nageku is from Old Japanese, verbalized from a noun for “sigh; lament” built from 長 (naga, “long”) plus 息 (iki, “breath”).
ダンプ is from English dump.
Utsuwa is from Old Japanese, cognate with 空 (utsuo), and appears to be 内 (utsu, “hollow”) plus は, though the は is unclear.
Neuchi is 値 (ne, “price; cost”) plus 打ち (uchi).
Sasuru is さ (sa) plus 擦る (suru, “to rub”), and the sa is unclear.
Obiru is from Old Japanese 帯ぶ (obu), which moved from the quadrigrade pattern to the upper bigrade and then to the modern upper monograde.
バッテリー is borrowed from English battery.
Tomobataraki is 共 (tomo-) plus 働き (hataraki), with hataraki voiced to bataraki by rendaku.
Arare is from Old Japanese and attested from the 8th century, and in the Man'yōshū it may mean small bits of hail or larger hailstones.
Shiageru is し (shi, “doing”) plus 上げる (ageru, “to raise up; to bring to an end”), from older 仕上ぐ (shiagu).
Nyō, “urine”, is ultimately from Middle Chinese 尿 (MC newH) and is first attested in 1275.
Chūdan is from Sinitic 中斷 (zhōngduàn).
Migurushii is 見 (mi, “looking”) plus 苦しい (kurushii, “painful, agonising”), with kurushii voiced to gurushii by rendaku.
Uruou may, on a surface analysis, be the irrealis of classical 潤ふ (urufu) plus ふ (fu), and it is related to 閏 (urū).
Hate is from the continuative stem of 果てる (hateru).
Omomuki is the continuative stem of the verb 趣く (omomuku).
Taihi is 対 (tai, “place in opposition and compare”) plus 比 (hi, “compare”).
Shiiru is from Old Japanese 強ふ (sipu), an upper bigrade verb, and is related to 誣いる (shiiru, “to slander; to defame”).
Hōwa is from Middle Chinese 飽和.
Shinjū is 心 (shin, “heart, mind, spirit”) plus 中 (-chū, “center, throughout”), with the chū voiced to jū.
ポット is from English pot.
